apoc_text: Then stood up Elias the prophet as fire, and his word burned like a lamp.
old_note: *Then stood up Elias the prophet as fire, and his word burned like a lamp.* Ecclesiasticus 48 opens the Hebrew library's explicit Praise of Elijah — the prophet-as-fire register that Matt 3:1's Yochanan (John) the Immerser walks in the Eliyahu (Elijah)-pattern. The pre-Christian Hebrew-library witness knew Eliyahu (Elijah) by the same fire-and-burning-word language Matthew's gospel inherits.
new_note: *Then stood up Elias the prophet as fire, and his word burned like a lamp.* (Ecclesiasticus 48:1). *In those days came John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness of Judaea,* (Matthew 3:1). Sirach opens his praise of Elijah with fire: he stood up as fire and his word burned like a lamp. Matthew opens John's ministry in the wilderness, and the fire is already there in what he says, *O generation of vipers* and *he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire* (Matthew 3:7, 11). The angel had told Zacharias his son would go before Yahuah (God) in the spirit and power of Elias (Luke 1:17), and Yahusha (Jesus) later says it plainly, *this is Elias, which was for to come* (Matthew 11:14). The prophet who stood up as fire has stood up again in the wilderness of Judaea.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 48:1 — *Then stood up Elias the prophet as fire, and his word burned like a lamp.* John comes preaching in the wilderness at Matthew 3:1 with the same fire in his word; he is the Elijah who was to come.

apoc_text: Who were ordained for reproofs in their times, to pacify the wrath of the judgment of Yahuah (God), before it brake forth into fury, and to turn the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.
old_note: *Who were ordained for reproofs in their times, to pacify the wrath of the judgment of Yahuah (God), before it brake forth into fury, and to turn the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.* Ecclesiasticus 48:10 echoes Malachi 4:5-6's *turn the heart of the fathers to the children* and explicitly adds *to restore the tribes of Jacob* — the gathering-of-the-scattered theme tied directly to the Eliyahu (Elijah)-pattern. The Hebrew library knew the promise carried the ingathering of all twelve tribes long before the gospel's opening verses; Yochanan's (John's) Yarden (Jordan) ministry stands in this register.
new_note: *Who were ordained for reproofs in their times, to pacify the wrath of the judgment of Yahuah (God), before it brake forth into fury, and to turn the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.* (Ecclesiasticus 48:10). *For this is he that was spoken of by the prophet Esaias, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of Yahuah (Lord), make his paths straight.* (Matthew 3:3). Sirach is drawing on Malachi, *he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children* (Malachi 4:6), and then he says what Malachi's Elijah is for: to restore the tribes of Jacob. Not Judah only, the tribes. That is the errand John steps into when he stands in the wilderness as the voice Isaiah heard, preparing the way of Yahuah (Lord). Preparing the way is the beginning of the Elijah work; the end of it is the scattered tribes of Jacob brought home, and the one whose way John prepared is the one who gathers them.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 48:10 — *to turn the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.* The Elijah errand ends in the restoring of the tribes of Jacob; the voice in the wilderness at Matthew 3:3 is its beginning.

apoc_text: Elias it was, who was covered with a whirlwind: and Eliseus was filled with his spirit: while he lived, he was not moved with the presence of any prince, neither could any bring him into subjection.
old_note: *Elias it was, who was covered with a whirlwind: and Eliseus was filled with his spirit: while he lived, he was not moved with the presence of any prince, neither could any bring him into subjection.* Ecclesiasticus 48:12 names the Eliyahu (Elijah) / Elisha mantle-transfer-by-spirit — at the Yarden (Jordan), the same river where Yahusha (Jesus) comes to Yochanan (John) at Matt 3:13. The river of the prophetic mantle is the river of the Messianic investiture; the Hebrew library witnesses the spirit-transfer at the Yarden the gospel inherits.
new_note: *Elias it was, who was covered with a whirlwind: and Eliseus was filled with his spirit: while he lived, he was not moved with the presence of any prince, neither could any bring him into subjection.* (Ecclesiasticus 48:12). *Then cometh Yahusha (Jesus) from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized of him.* (Matthew 3:13). The whirlwind took Elijah at the Jordan, and Elisha came back across the same river carrying his spirit (2 Kings 2:8–15). Sirach adds that no prince could move Elijah while he lived. Now Yahusha (Jesus) comes from Galilee to the Jordan, to a man no prince could move either, the John who would shortly tell Herod his marriage was unlawful. At that river the heavens open and the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit) comes down on him (Matthew 3:16). The Jordan is where the prophetic spirit passed from Elijah to Elisha, and it is where the Spirit rests on the one Elijah's successor was sent to announce.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 48:12 — *Elias it was, who was covered with a whirlwind: and Eliseus was filled with his spirit.* The spirit passed from Elijah to Elisha at the Jordan; at Matthew 3:13 Yahusha (Jesus) comes to the same river and the Spirit descends.

apoc_text: He professeth to have the knowledge of Yahuah (God): and he calls himself the child of Yahuah (God).
old_note: *He professeth to have the knowledge of Yahuah (God): and he calleth himself the child of Yahuah (the Lord).* Wisdom of Solomon 2:13 names the Hebrew library's framework for the testing-of-the-righteous-one: the ungodly identify the righteous-one by his claim to be the child of Yahuah and plot to test that claim. Matt 4:3's *if thou be the Son of Elohim (God)* is the devil's instance of the same testing-by-challenge-of-the-Sonship pattern. The Wisdom architecture sets the literary register the temptation pericope walks at the Messianic level.
new_note: *He professeth to have the knowledge of Yahuah (God): and he calls himself the child of Yahuah (God).* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:13). *And when the tempter came to him, he said, If thou be the Son of Elohim (God), command that these stones be made bread.* (Matthew 4:3). The ungodly in Wisdom of Solomon fasten on one claim, that the righteous man calls himself the child of Yahuah (God), and they set out to test it: *if the just man be the son of God, he will help him* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:18). The tempter in the wilderness uses the same handle, if you are the Son of Elohim (God), prove it, command the stones. The test comes back at the cross in the same words, *If thou be the Son of Elohim (God), come down from the cross* (Matthew 27:40). The claim of sonship is what the ungodly cannot leave alone, and the devil was the first to pick it up.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 2:13 — *he calls himself the child of Yahuah (God).* The ungodly test the righteous one's claim to be the child of Yahuah (God); the tempter at Matthew 4:3 says if thou be the Son.

apoc_text: We are esteemed of him as counterfeits: he abstaineth from our ways as from filthiness: he pronounceth the end of the just to be blessed, and makes his boast that Yahuah (God) is his father.
old_note: *We are esteemed of him as counterfeits: he abstaineth from our ways as from filthiness: he pronounceth the end of the just to be blessed, and maketh his boast that Elohim (God) is his father.* Wisdom 2:16 names the ungodly's frame: the righteous-one boasts that Elohim is his father, and the ungodly resent the boast. Matt 4:6's *if thou be the Son of Elohim, cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee* enacts the same testing-of-the-claimed-Sonship dynamic — demanding visible proof of the Father's protection from the one who has claimed Elohim as his father.
new_note: *We are esteemed of him as counterfeits: he abstaineth from our ways as from filthiness: he pronounceth the end of the just to be blessed, and makes his boast that Yahuah (God) is his father.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:16). *And saith unto him, If thou be the Son of Elohim (God), cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee: and in their hands they shall bear thee up, lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone.* (Matthew 4:6). The ungodly resent one thing above the rest: the righteous man makes his boast that Yahuah (God) is his father. In the wilderness the tempter picks up the same grievance and turns it into a dare — if you are the Son of Elohim (God), prove it, throw yourself down and let the angels catch you. The claim of sonship is treated as something to be tested by a display of rescue. Yahusha (Jesus) did not take the dare, because sonship is shown by doing the Father's will, not by forcing the Father's hand.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 2:16 — *makes his boast that Yahuah (God) is his father.* The boast the ungodly resent is the claim the tempter dares him to prove at Matthew 4:6.

apoc_text: For if the just man be the son of Yahuah (God), he will help him, and deliver him from the hand of his enemies.
old_note: *For if the just man be the Son of Elohim (God), he will help him, and deliver him from the hand of his enemies.* Wisdom 2:18 is the Hebrew library's direct prefiguring of Matt 4:6 — the ungodly's *let-Elohim-save-him-if-he-is-his* testing-pattern. Wisdom names the architecture; Matt 4:6 walks it at the Messianic level; the devil's cut-quote of Psalm 91 is the *let-the-angels-save-him* instance of the Wisdom pattern.
new_note: *For if the just man be the son of Yahuah (God), he will help him, and deliver him from the hand of his enemies.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:18). *And saith unto him, If thou be the Son of Elohim (God), cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee: and in their hands they shall bear thee up, lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone.* (Matthew 4:6). Wisdom puts the test in the mouths of the ungodly: if he really is the son of Yahuah (God), then his Father will have to rescue him. The devil carries the same test into the wilderness almost word for word — if thou be the Son of Elohim (God), cast thyself down, and let the angels bear thee up. He even cuts a line out of Psalm 91 to make the dare sound like scripture. The writer of Wisdom had heard this voice centuries before; the gospel shows whose voice it is.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 2:18 — *if the just man be the son of Yahuah (God), he will help him.* The ungodly's test is the devil's dare at Matthew 4:6, down to the cut quotation of Psalm 91.

apoc_text: Let us condemn him with a shameful death: for by his own saying he shall be respected.
old_note: *Let us condemn him with a shameful death: for by his own saying he shall be respected.* Wisdom 2:20 names the death-sentence-against-the-righteous-one that the ungodly's plot culminates in. Matt 4:11's *Then the devil leaveth him* names the wilderness-end of the first phase of the plot; the Wisdom architecture extends past the wilderness through the gospel's whole arc to the cross. The Hebrew library names the full arc the gospel will walk; the temptation is the opening.
new_note: *Let us condemn him with a shameful death: for by his own saying he shall be respected.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:20). *Then the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him.* (Matthew 4:11). The plot against the righteous man in Wisdom ends in a death sentence; the plot against Yahusha (Jesus) in the wilderness ends with the devil leaving and angels ministering to him. The two are not in conflict. The wilderness was the opening move, not the last one — the enemy withdrew to come back through other hands. Wisdom names the whole arc from reproof to shameful death; Matthew 4 is where that arc begins in the gospel, and it does not end until the cross.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 2:20 — *Let us condemn him with a shameful death.* The plot's end; Matthew 4:11's *Then the devil leaveth him* is only the end of its first round.

apoc_text: But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of Yahuah (God), and there shall no torment touch them.
old_note: *But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of Yahuah (God), and there shall no torment touch them.* Wisdom of Solomon 3:1 names the protection-of-the-righteous register the persecuted-for-righteousness Beatitude carries forward. Matt 5:10-12's *blessed are they which are persecuted ... rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven* walks the same architecture: the persecution lands on the body, the soul rests in the Father's hand. The Hebrew library names the substance that Yahusha (Jesus) extends into the Beatitude.
new_note: *But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of Yahuah (God), and there shall no torment touch them.* (Wisdom of Solomon 3:1). *Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness’ sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.* (Matthew 5:10). Wisdom's third chapter answers its second. The ungodly tortured and condemned the righteous, and here is where the righteous ended up: in the hand of Yahuah (God), where no torment can reach them. Yahusha (Jesus) says the same to those persecuted for righteousness' sake — the kingdom is theirs. The persecution lands on the body and goes no further. What Wisdom promised the just man, the King promised everyone who would be hated for walking as he walked.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 3:1 — *the souls of the righteous are in the hand of Yahuah (God), and there shall no torment touch them.* Where the persecuted of Matthew 5:10 end up — theirs is the kingdom.

apoc_text: They that put their trust in him shall understand the truth: and such as be faithful in love shall abide with him: for grace and mercy is to his saints, and he has care for his elect.
old_note: *They that put their trust in him shall understand the truth: and such as be faithful in love shall abide with him: for grace and mercy is to his saints, and he has care for his elect.* Wisdom 3:9 names the great-is-your-reward register — *grace and mercy is to his saints, and he has care for his elect.* Matt 5:12's *great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you* walks the same Hebrew library reward-and-care promise on the elect, extended to the disciples joining the prophetic-witness lineage.
new_note: *They that put their trust in him shall understand the truth: and such as be faithful in love shall abide with him: for grace and mercy is to his saints, and he has care for his elect.* (Wisdom of Solomon 3:9). *Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you.* (Matthew 5:12). Wisdom closes its word to the persecuted righteous with what they have coming: understanding of the truth, abiding with him, grace and mercy to his saints, and his care over his elect. Yahusha (Jesus) says the same to his disciples — rejoice, for great is your reward in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets before you. The disciples are being added to the line of the prophets who were hated for speaking the Father's word, and the care and reward Wisdom promised the elect is laid up for them in the same place.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 3:9 — *grace and mercy is to his saints, and he has care for his elect.* The reward laid up for the persecuted at Matthew 5:12, who join the line of the prophets.

apoc_text: Accustom not your mouth to swearing; neither use thyself to the naming of the Holy One.
old_note: *Accustom not your mouth to swearing; neither use thyself to the naming of the Holy One.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 23:9 names the oath-restraint register the Hebrew library carries — the wisdom-counsel against the casual oath-formula apparatus. Matt 5:33-37's *swear not at all ... let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay* walks the same Hebrew library register at the heart-Torah level: cut the gradation-evasion apparatus, restore the integrity of speech the Torah commands.
new_note: *Accustom not your mouth to swearing; neither use thyself to the naming of the Holy One.* (Ecclesiasticus 23:9). *Again, ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time, Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto Yahuah (Lord) thine oaths:* (Matthew 5:33). Sirach tells his son not to let his mouth grow used to swearing, nor to make a habit of naming the Holy One. Yahusha (Jesus) begins from what they had heard said of old — do not forswear yourself, perform your oaths to Yahuah (Lord) — and goes on to say swear not at all, let your yes be yes and your no be no. He is not loosening the Torah on oaths; he is cutting away the habit Sirach warned of, the casual oath that made the name common and the word cheap. Speech that is true needs no oath to prop it up.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 23:9 — *Accustom not your mouth to swearing.* The casual oath Sirach warns against is what Matthew 5:33 begins to cut away.

apoc_text: For as a servant that is continually beaten shall not be without a blue mark: so he that sweareth and nameth Yahuah (God) continually shall not be faultless.
old_note: *For as a servant that is continually beaten shall not be without a blue mark: so he that sweareth and nameth Yahuah (God) continually shall not be faultless.* Sirach 23:10 names the standing-consequence of habitual oath-taking — the moral-mark left by the practice. Matt 5:34's *swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is Elohim's (God's) throne* walks the same architecture: the casual invocation of the heavenly things in the oath-apparatus is the standing diminishment the Hebrew library has already named.
new_note: *For as a servant that is continually beaten shall not be without a blue mark: so he that sweareth and nameth Yahuah (God) continually shall not be faultless.* (Ecclesiasticus 23:10). *But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is Elohim's (God’s) throne:* (Matthew 5:34). Sirach says a servant who is beaten every day is never without a bruise, and a man who swears and names Yahuah (God) continually is never clean of fault — the habit leaves its mark. Yahusha (Jesus) says swear not at all, not even by heaven, because heaven is the throne of Elohim (God). To swear by heaven lightly is to drag the throne into common talk. The mark Sirach describes is what casual swearing does to a man, and the command in Matthew is how it stops.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 23:10 — *he that sweareth and nameth Yahuah (God) continually shall not be faultless.* The mark habitual swearing leaves; *Swear not at all; neither by heaven* (Matthew 5:34).

apoc_text: A man that useth much swearing shall be filled with iniquity, and the plague shall never depart from his house: if he shall offend, his sin shall be upon him: and if he acknowledge not his sin, he makes a double offence: and if he swear in vain, he shall not be innocent, but his house shall be full of calamities.
old_note: *A man that useth much swearing shall be filled with iniquity, and the plague shall never depart from his house: if he shall offend, his sin shall be upon him: and if he acknowledge not his sin, he maketh a double offence.* Sirach 23:11 names the cumulative-iniquity of the oath-apparatus user — the plague that does not depart. Matt 5:37's *let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil* lands the same diagnostic at the heart-Torah level: the gradation-evasion apparatus *cometh of evil* — the Hebrew library's *filled with iniquity* in gospel-grammar.
new_note: *A man that useth much swearing shall be filled with iniquity, and the plague shall never depart from his house: if he shall offend, his sin shall be upon him: and if he acknowledge not his sin, he makes a double offence: and if he swear in vain, he shall not be innocent, but his house shall be full of calamities.* (Ecclesiasticus 23:11). *But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.* (Matthew 5:37). Sirach traces what much swearing does to a man: he is filled with iniquity, the plague does not leave his house, and every oath sworn in vain adds to the account. Yahusha (Jesus) names the root in one line — whatever is more than yes and no comes of evil. The iniquity Sirach saw filling the swearer's house and the evil Yahusha (Jesus) names at the source are the same thing seen from two ends. Plain speech, yes and no, is the way out of both.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 23:11 — *A man that useth much swearing shall be filled with iniquity.* The iniquity that fills the swearer is the evil Matthew 5:37 names at the root.

apoc_text: But by such works have you taught your people that the just man should be merciful, and have made your children to be of a good hope that you give repentance for sins.
old_note: *But by such works have you taught your people that the just man should be merciful, and have made your children to be of a good hope that you give repentance for sins.* Wisdom of Solomon 12:19 names the Father's mercy-pattern as the teaching-source of the just-man-should-be-merciful ethic. Matt 5:44-45's *love your enemies, bless them that curse you ... that ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust* walks the same Father-pattern architecture: the Father's mercy on enemies teaches the children the ethic the children walk.
new_note: *But by such works have you taught your people that the just man should be merciful, and have made your children to be of a good hope that you give repentance for sins.* (Wisdom of Solomon 12:19). *But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;* (Matthew 5:44). Solomon says the Father's dealings with Yashar'el's (Israel's) enemies were themselves the lesson: by such works he taught his people that the just man should be merciful, and gave his children good hope that he gives repentance for sins. The King teaches the same lesson from the same source. Love your enemies, bless those who curse you, pray for those who persecute you, and the reason follows in the next verse: so that you may be children of your Father, who does exactly that. The mercy the children show is learned from watching the Father show it.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 12:19 — *by such works have you taught your people that the just man should be merciful.* Love your enemies (Matthew 5:44) is the lesson the Father taught by his own mercy on enemies.

apoc_text: For if you did punish the enemies of your children, and the condemned to death, with such deliberation, giving them time and place, by which they might be delivered from their malice:
old_note: *For if you did punish the enemies of your children, and the condemned to death, with such deliberation, giving them time and place, by which they might be delivered from their malice.* Wisdom 12:20 names the Father's long-suffering-toward-enemies pattern — punishment carried with deliberation, time and place given for repentance. Matt 5:45's *he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust* walks the same Hebrew library pattern: the Father's standing mercy on the evil-still-given-time is the pattern the gathered children imitate when they love their personal enemies in the present age.
new_note: *For if you did punish the enemies of your children, and the condemned to death, with such deliberation, giving them time and place, by which they might be delivered from their malice:* (Wisdom of Solomon 12:20). *That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.* (Matthew 5:45). Even the enemies of his children, even those already condemned to death, he punished with deliberation, giving them time and place to be delivered from their malice. The King points at the sky for the same pattern: the Father makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. The wicked are still being given daylight and harvest, which is time and place to turn. Children who love their enemies in this age are copying a Father who has been doing it since before the land was given.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 12:20 — *giving them time and place, by which they might be delivered from their malice.* Sun on the evil and rain on the unjust (Matthew 5:45) is the time and place the Father gives enemies to turn.

apoc_text: The offering of the righteous makes the altar fat, and the sweet savour thereof is before the Most High.
old_note: *The offering of the righteous makes the altar fat, and the sweet savour thereof is before the Most High.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 35:6 names the architecture of the righteous-offering-accepted-by-the-Most-High that Matt 6:4's *thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly* walks at the heart-level. The Hebrew library names the offering itself; the gospel names the heart-form of the offering: the secret-act of the kingdom-citizen reaches the same Most High the wisdom-stream named as receiving the offering of the righteous.
new_note: *The offering of the righteous makes the altar fat, and the sweet savour thereof is before the Most High.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:6). *That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.* (Matthew 6:4). Sirach says the offering of the righteous makes the altar fat and its sweet savour rises before the Most High. Yahusha (Jesus) says alms given in secret are seen by the Father who sees in secret, and he rewards them openly. The altar is the same in both: it is the Most High who receives, and he receives what is righteous, not what is displayed. An offering made for men to see never reaches that altar; the one made where only he looks is the sweet savour.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 35:6 — *the sweet savour thereof is before the Most High.* Alms in secret (Matthew 6:4) reach the same Most High who receives the righteous offering.

apoc_text: The sacrifice of a just man is acceptable. and the memorial thereof shall never be forgotten.
old_note: *The sacrifice of a just man is acceptable, and the memorial thereof shall never be forgotten.* Sirach 35:7 names the *memorial shall never be forgotten* register the Father's reward-economy at Matt 6:4 carries. The Pharisaic-counterfeit form trades the eternal memorial for the brief currency of being-seen-of-men; the kingdom-citizens form lays up what the Most High does not forget. The Hebrew library names the architecture the gospel walks.
new_note: *The sacrifice of a just man is acceptable. and the memorial thereof shall never be forgotten.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:7). *That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.* (Matthew 6:4). Sirach says the sacrifice of a just man is accepted and its memorial is never forgotten. Yahusha (Jesus) says alms given in secret are seen by the Father, who repays openly. The reward of being seen by men is spent the moment it is received; the memorial Sirach speaks of is kept by the Most High, who does not forget. The just man's offering goes into a record that outlasts him.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 35:7 — *the memorial thereof shall never be forgotten.* The Father who sees in secret (Matthew 6:4) keeps the memorial men never saw.
writer_flag: Live text misprint: Ecclesiasticus 35:7 reads 'acceptable. and the memorial' (period for comma); quoted as it stands.

apoc_text: Forgive your neighbour the hurt that he has done to you, so shall your sins also be forgiven when you prayest.
old_note: *Forgive your neighbour the hurt that he has done to you, so shall your sins also be forgiven when you prayest.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 28:2 names the conditional-forgiveness architecture explicitly in the wisdom-stream — the receiving of pardon from the Most High presupposes the extending of pardon to the neighbour, named in the same act of praying. This is the direct architectural parallel to Matt 6:12's *forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.* The Hebrew library was already teaching the kingdom-citizens prayer-pattern at the verse-level; the Lord's Prayer walks the same architecture.
new_note: *Forgive your neighbour the hurt that he has done to you, so shall your sins also be forgiven when you prayest.* (Ecclesiasticus 28:2). *And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.* (Matthew 6:12). Sirach says forgive your neighbour the hurt he did you, and then your own sins will be forgiven when you pray. That is the petition Yahusha (Jesus) taught his disciples to pray, forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors, and the condition is the same in both. Pardon received and pardon extended are named in one breath, in the same act of prayer. The disciples' prayer was not a new idea in Yashar'el (Israel); the wise had been teaching sons to pray this way for generations.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:2 — *so shall your sins also be forgiven when you prayest.* Forgiveness asked for and forgiveness given in one prayer; *forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors* (Matthew 6:12).

apoc_text: He sheweth no mercy to a man, which is like himself: and does he ask forgiveness of his own sins?
old_note: *He sheweth no mercy to a man, which is like himself: and does he ask forgiveness of his own sins?* Sirach 28:4 lands the diagnostic at the heart-level — the brother-who-is-like-thee is the test of the heart that asks the Father's mercy. Matt 6:15's *if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses* walks the same Hebrew library architecture: the unforgiving heart cannot rightly ask the forgiveness it withholds. The wisdom-stream had already named the condition the Lord's Prayer formalizes.
new_note: *He sheweth no mercy to a man, which is like himself: and does he ask forgiveness of his own sins?* (Ecclesiasticus 28:4). *But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.* (Matthew 6:15). Sirach presses the question down to the heart: a man shows no mercy to another man, one made like himself, and then asks forgiveness for his own sins? Yahusha (Jesus) answers it in the Sermon: if you forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive yours. The brother who is like you is the test. The heart that withholds mercy from him has no standing to ask it from the Father, and the wise in Yashar'el (Israel) had been saying so long before the disciples' prayer was taught.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:4 — *He sheweth no mercy to a man, which is like himself.* No mercy to the man like yourself, no forgiveness to ask; *if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive* (Matthew 6:15).

apoc_text: Because that alms do deliver from death, and suffers not to come into darkness.
old_note: *Because that alms do deliver from death, and suffers not to come into darkness.* Tobit 4:10 names the alms-as-deliverer-from-death architecture — the treasure laid up by the open hand protects the giver at the day of necessity. Matt 6:20's *treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal* walks the same protection-against-loss architecture at the heavenly-treasure level. The Hebrew library names the deliverance the open hand purchases; the gospel names the corruption-proof storehouse the open hand fills.
new_note: *Because that alms do deliver from death, and suffers not to come into darkness.* (Tobit 4:10). *But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:* (Matthew 6:20). Tobit tells his son that alms deliver from death and keep a man out of the darkness; the open hand protects the giver in the day of necessity. Yahusha (Jesus) says to lay up treasure in heaven, where moth and rust do not corrupt and thieves do not break through. Both are talking about what cannot be lost. The library names the deliverance the open hand brings; the gospel names the storehouse the open hand fills, and nothing gets in to spoil it.
member_note: Tobit 4:10 — *alms do deliver from death, and suffers not to come into darkness.* The deliverance the open hand brings, stored where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt (Matthew 6:20).

apoc_text: Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High, and it shall bring you more profit than gold.
old_note: *Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High, and it shall bring you more profit than gold.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 29:11 names the *lay up your treasure* architecture explicitly with the commandment-keeping the gospel's kingdom-citizens righteousness presupposes. Matt 6:20's *lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven* is the gospel-form of the wisdom-stream's same teaching: the treasure laid up by the open hand of the commandment-keeper is the heavenly-treasure the gospel names.
new_note: *Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High, and it shall bring you more profit than gold.* (Ecclesiasticus 29:11). *But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:* (Matthew 6:20). Sirach says lay up your treasure the way the commandments of the Most High direct, and it will profit you more than gold. Yahusha (Jesus) says lay up for yourselves treasure in heaven, where moth and rust and thieves cannot reach. The two are the same counsel: the hand that opens to the brother and the poor because the commandment says so is laying up the treasure the King means. The treasure in heaven is kept by keeping the commandments on earth.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 29:11 — *Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High.* The treasure laid up by the open hand of the commandment keeper is the *treasures in heaven* of Matthew 6:20.

apoc_text: Give Yahuah (God) his honour with a good eye, and diminish not the firstfruits of yours hands.
old_note: *Give Yahuah (God) his honour with a good eye, and diminish not the firstfruits of yours hands.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 35:8 names the *good eye* in giving — the wisdom-stream's direct linguistic anchor for the gospel's *single eye* idiom. The Hebrew *tov-ayin* (good of eye) is rendered into Greek and into English along the architecture the gospel walks: give with a *good eye,* not stinted, not held-back. Matt 6:22's *single eye* full of light is the gospel-grammar form of the wisdom-stream's *good eye* in giving.
new_note: *Give Yahuah (God) his honour with a good eye, and diminish not the firstfruits of yours hands.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:8). *The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.* (Matthew 6:22). Sirach tells the worshipper to give Yahuah (God) his honour with a good eye and not to cut short the firstfruits of his hands. The good eye is an old Hebrew way of speaking of generosity, the eye that is not grudging and does not measure what it gives. Yahusha (Jesus) speaks of the single eye that fills the whole body with light, and the verses around it are about treasure and about mammon. A good eye in giving and a single eye in the body are the same eye; it looks at Yahuah (God) and his honour, and the hand follows where it looks.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 35:8 — *Give Yahuah (God) his honour with a good eye.* The good eye in giving is the single eye of Matthew 6:22.

apoc_text: The envious man has a wicked eye; he turns away his face, and despiseth men.
old_note: *The envious man has a wicked eye; he turns away his face, and despiseth men.* Sirach 14:8 names the *wicked eye* of envy as the Hebrew library's parallel to Matt 6:23's *evil eye.* The wisdom-stream identifies the wicked-eye not as a generic spiritual-vision metaphor but as the envious/stingy heart that turns its face away and despiseth — the closed hand. Matt 6:23 walks the same Hebrew-idiom architecture.
new_note: *The envious man has a wicked eye; he turns away his face, and despiseth men.* (Ecclesiasticus 14:8). *But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!* (Matthew 6:23). Sirach calls envy a wicked eye and says the man who has it turns away his face and despises men. Yahusha (Jesus) says the evil eye fills the whole body with darkness. In the Hebrew idiom the evil eye is not a vague picture of bad vision; it is the stingy, envious heart that closes its hand and looks away. The King is speaking the idiom Sirach spoke, and the darkness he names is the darkness of the closed hand.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 14:8 — *The envious man has a wicked eye.* Sirach's wicked eye of envy is the evil eye that darkens the body at Matthew 6:23.

apoc_text: A covetous man’s eye is not satisfied with his portion; and the iniquity of the wicked drieth up his soul.
old_note: *A covetous man's eye is not satisfied with his portion; and the iniquity of the wicked drieth up his soul.* Sirach 14:9 names the covetous-eye-is-not-satisfied architecture — the grasping heart that never has enough is the same heart the gospel names at Matt 6:23. The *whole body full of darkness* of the evil-eye reader is the *iniquity that drieth up the soul* of the wisdom-stream reader. The Hebrew library has been naming the diagnostic for centuries; the gospel walks the same diagnostic.
new_note: *A covetous man’s eye is not satisfied with his portion; and the iniquity of the wicked drieth up his soul.* (Ecclesiasticus 14:9). *But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!* (Matthew 6:23). Sirach says the covetous eye is never satisfied with its portion, and that the iniquity dries the soul up. Yahusha (Jesus) says the evil eye leaves the whole body full of darkness. A dried-up soul and a darkened body are two ways of describing one man — the grasping one who never has enough and cannot see by his own light.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 14:9 — *A covetous man’s eye is not satisfied with his portion.* The unsatisfied eye that dries the soul is the evil eye of Matthew 6:23.

apoc_text: A wicked eye envies his bread, and he is a niggard at his table.
old_note: *A wicked eye envies his bread, and he is a niggard at his table.* Sirach 14:10 names the wicked-eye-at-the-table architecture — the host who serves bread while begrudging it; the food eaten is unblessed because the heart is closed. Matt 6:23's *if therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!* walks the same intensity-of-the-darkness diagnostic the Hebrew library names: the closed-heart host's whole hospitality is darkness, no matter how much bread crosses the table.
new_note: *A wicked eye envies his bread, and he is a niggard at his table.* (Ecclesiasticus 14:10). *But if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in thee be darkness, how great is that darkness!* (Matthew 6:23). Sirach brings the wicked eye to the table: the host who begrudges his own bread even as he serves it. Yahusha (Jesus) asks how great the darkness is when the light itself has gone dark. Bread can cross a table with no blessing in it. The niggard's whole hospitality is darkness, however much he puts out, because the eye behind it is closed.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 14:10 — *A wicked eye envies his bread, and he is a niggard at his table.* The niggard's table is the darkness of Matthew 6:23 with bread on it.

apoc_text: He that loves gold shall not be justified, and he that followeth corruption shall have enough thereof.
old_note: *He that loves gold shall not be justified, and he that followeth corruption shall have enough thereof.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 31:5 names the architecture of gold-love-disqualifies-from-justification — the Hebrew library's direct anti-Mammon teaching. Matt 6:24's *ye cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon* walks the same architecture at the kingdom-citizens level: the gold-lover cannot stand justified before the Father whose service is whole-heart.
new_note: *He that loves gold shall not be justified, and he that followeth corruption shall have enough thereof.* (Ecclesiasticus 31:5). *No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon.* (Matthew 6:24). Sirach says the man who loves gold will not be justified. Yahusha (Jesus) says why: no man can serve two masters, and you cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon. The man whose heart holds to gold has already given his service to another master, and he cannot stand justified before a Father whose service is the whole heart. The gold-lover and the mammon-server are the same man seen from two sides.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 31:5 — *He that loves gold shall not be justified, and he that followeth corruption.* The gold-lover cannot stand justified because *ye cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon* (Matthew 6:24).

apoc_text: Gold has been the ruin of many, and their destruction was present.
old_note: *Gold has been the ruin of many, and their destruction was present.* Sirach 31:6 names the gold-as-ruin diagnostic the wisdom-stream carried. Matt 6:24's forced-choice between Yahuah (God) and Mammon is the present-age form of the same wisdom: the disciple who chooses Mammon walks toward the same ruin the wisdom-stream had been naming.
new_note: *Gold has been the ruin of many, and their destruction was present.* (Ecclesiasticus 31:6). *No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon.* (Matthew 6:24). Sirach says gold has ruined many, and their destruction was right there with it. Yahusha (Jesus) sets the choice before his disciples: Elohim (God) or mammon, one master or the other, never both. The disciple who chooses mammon is walking toward the ruin Sirach had already watched overtake many. The wise saw where gold leads; the King made the fork in the road plain.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 31:6 — *Gold has been the ruin of many, and their destruction was present.* Where gold leads; the choice between Elohim (God) and mammon at Matthew 6:24 is the fork before that ruin.

apoc_text: It is a stumblingblock to them that sacrifice to it, and every fool shall be taken with it.
old_note: *It is a stumblingblock to them that sacrifice to it, and every fool shall be taken with it.* Sirach 31:7 names gold-as-stumblingblock-for-those-who-sacrifice-to-it — the wisdom-stream's direct identification of wealth as an object of worship that captures its devotees. Matt 6:24 walks the same architecture at the Mammon-or-Elohim binary: Mammon is treated as a competing master because the gold-sacrificers of the wisdom-stream had already named it as a master that takes its devotees.
new_note: *It is a stumblingblock to them that sacrifice to it, and every fool shall be taken with it.* (Ecclesiasticus 31:7). *No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon.* (Matthew 6:24). Sirach speaks of men who sacrifice to gold. He names it as a thing worshipped, an altar men bring offerings to, and he says it trips every fool who goes near it. That is why Yahusha (Jesus) can set mammon across from Elohim (God) as a rival master: mammon in that sentence is not a neutral tool but a master that takes those who serve it, the very stumblingblock Sirach saw men sacrificing to. You cannot keep an altar to both.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 31:7 — *It is a stumblingblock to them that sacrifice to it.* Gold as a master men sacrifice to; *Ye cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon* (Matthew 6:24).

apoc_text: But the righteous live for evermore; their reward also is with Yahuah (God), and the care of them is with the Most High.
old_note: *But the righteous live for evermore; their reward also is with Yahuah (God), and the care of them is with the Most High.* Wisdom of Solomon 5:15 names the care-of-the-righteous-is-with-the-Most-High architecture the take-no-thought teaching of Matt 6:25-26 grounds itself in. The Hebrew library names the Father's standing care for the righteous; the gospel names the practice that follows from that care: the kingdom-citizens do not anxiously grasp because the Most High's care is already with them.
new_note: *But the righteous live for evermore; their reward also is with Yahuah (God), and the care of them is with the Most High.* (Wisdom of Solomon 5:15). *Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?* (Matthew 6:26). The care of the righteous is with the Most High. That is the ground the King stands on when he tells his disciples to look at the birds: they neither sow nor reap nor fill barns, and the heavenly Father feeds them, and you are worth more than they. Taking no anxious thought is not a technique; it is what follows when you know whose care you are already in. Solomon named the care, and the King named the birds so his hearers could see it with their eyes.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 5:15 — *the care of them is with the Most High.* The Father who feeds the birds (Matthew 6:26) is the Most High whose care the righteous are already in.

apoc_text: Therefore shall they receive a glorious kingdom, and a beautiful crown from the hand of Yahuah (God): for with his right hand shall he cover them, and with his arm shall he protect them.
old_note: *Therefore shall they receive a glorious kingdom, and a beautiful crown from the hand of Yahuah (God): for with his right hand shall he cover them, and with his arm shall he protect them.* Wisdom 5:16 names the glorious-kingdom-from-the-Father's-hand architecture and the right-hand-covering / arm-protecting protection-economy of the righteous. Matt 6:33's *seek ye first the kingdom of Elohim (God), and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you* walks the same architecture: the kingdom received from the Father's hand carries the daily-provision the seeker does not have to grasp for.
new_note: *Therefore shall they receive a glorious kingdom, and a beautiful crown from the hand of Yahuah (God): for with his right hand shall he cover them, and with his arm shall he protect them.* (Wisdom of Solomon 5:16). *But seek ye first the kingdom of Elohim (God), and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.* (Matthew 6:33). The kingdom and the crown come from the hand of Yahuah (God), and his right hand covers those who receive them. The King tells his disciples to seek that kingdom first and let the rest be added. Food and clothing are the small things the covering hand already holds for the one who is reaching for the kingdom itself; the same arm that protects the righteous in Wisdom is the one the King promises will add all these things.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 5:16 — *Therefore shall they receive a glorious kingdom, and a beautiful crown from the hand of Yahuah (God).* Seek the kingdom first (Matthew 6:33); the kingdom and the crown come from the Father's hand, and all the rest is added.

apoc_text: Prosperity and adversity, life and death, poverty and riches, come of Yahuah (God).
old_note: *Prosperity and adversity, life and death, poverty and riches, come of Yahuah (God).* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 11:14 names the all-comes-of-Yahuah architecture the daily-provision trust of the seek-first teaching presupposes. Matt 6:33's *all these things shall be added unto you* walks the same Hebrew library architecture: the Father is the source of both prosperity and adversity; the kingdom-citizens orientation toward the kingdom carries through both because the Father administers both.
new_note: *Prosperity and adversity, life and death, poverty and riches, come of Yahuah (God).* (Ecclesiasticus 11:14). *But seek ye first the kingdom of Elohim (God), and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.* (Matthew 6:33). Sirach says both halves come from Yahuah (God) — prosperity and adversity, life and death, poverty and riches. That is the ground under Yahusha's (Jesus's) seek first: if the Father administers both, the citizen does not have to administer either, and can turn toward the kingdom and his righteousness with both hands. The adding comes from the same hand the adversity does.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 11:14 — *Prosperity and adversity, life and death, poverty and riches, come of Yahuah (God).* Because both come of Yahuah (God), the citizen can seek first the kingdom at Matthew 6:33.

apoc_text: Do that to no man which you hatest: drink not wine to make you drunken: neither let drunkenness go with you in your journey.
old_note: *Do that to no man which thou hatest: drink not wine to make thee drunken: neither let drunkenness go with thee in thy journey.* Tobit 4:15 carries the Golden Rule in the Hebrew library, articulated in negative form by the angel Raphael's closing instruction to Tobias — centuries before the Sermon on the Mount. Matt 7:12 walks the same teaching in positive form (*all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them*) and binds it to the Sermon's whole architecture by *for this is the law and the prophets.* The Christian-supersessionism reading that treats Yahusha (Jesus) as the innovator of a brand-new ethic replacing an allegedly *complicated* Tanakh collapses against Tobit 4:15. The teaching was already in the Hebrew library; the King restores it as the heart-substance of the Torah and the prophets.
new_note: *Do that to no man which you hatest: drink not wine to make you drunken: neither let drunkenness go with you in your journey.* (Tobit 4:15). *Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.* (Matthew 7:12). Here is the golden rule in the Hebrew library, in its negative form, from a father to his son generations before the Sermon on the Mount. Yahusha (Jesus) states it positively and then says what it is: *this is the law and the prophets.* He was not bringing a kinder ethic to replace a Torah too hard to keep; he was naming the heart of the Torah that Tobit had already handed to his son. The teaching that the King invented a new religion in place of the law collapses against this one verse in Tobit.
member_note: Tobit 4:15 — *Do that to no man which you hatest.* The golden rule in negative form, generations before *this is the law and the prophets* (Matthew 7:12).
writer_flag: Corrected the old note: it attributed Tobit 4:15 to 'the angel Raphael's closing instruction to Tobias'. Tobit 4 is Tobit the father instructing his son; Raphael's instruction is Tobit 12.

apoc_text: Malice and wrath, even these are abominations; and the sinful man shall have them both.
old_note: *Malice and wrath, even these are abominations; and the sinful man shall have them both.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 27:30 names the heart-condition that the just-judgment architecture of Matt 7:1-2 requires to be cleared first. The wisdom-stream identifies malice and wrath as abominations the sinful man carries; the kingdom-citizens judge-not-that-ye-be-not-judged teaching presupposes the same diagnostic — the carrier of malice cannot judge the brother rightly, because the *with what judgment ye judge* standard rebounds on the carrier.
new_note: *Malice and wrath, even these are abominations; and the sinful man shall have them both.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:30). *Judge not, that ye be not judged.* (Matthew 7:1). Sirach calls malice and wrath abominations and says the sinful man carries both. Yahusha (Jesus) says judge not, that you be not judged, and the next verse tells why: the measure you use is the measure that comes back on you. A man carrying malice cannot judge his brother rightly, because the malice is in the judgment, and the judgment rebounds. Sirach names the heart condition that has to be cleared before any brother can be weighed.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 27:30 — *Malice and wrath, even these are abominations.* The heart condition that has to go before a brother is weighed; *judge not, that ye be not judged* (Matthew 7:1).

apoc_text: He that revengeth shall find vengeance from Yahuah (God), and he will surely keep his sins in remembrance.
old_note: *He that revengeth shall find vengeance from Yahuah (God), and he will surely keep his sins in remembrance.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 28:1 names the measure-for-measure architecture explicitly in the Hebrew library — the revenger receives vengeance from the Most High, and the Father remembers his sins. Matt 7:2's *with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again* walks the same wisdom-stream architecture at the kingdom-citizens level: the standard the disciple applies to others is the standard the Father applies to the disciple.
new_note: *He that revengeth shall find vengeance from Yahuah (God), and he will surely keep his sins in remembrance.* (Ecclesiasticus 28:1). *For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.* (Matthew 7:2). Sirach says the man who takes revenge will get vengeance from Yahuah (God), and his own sins will be kept in remembrance. Yahusha (Jesus) says it as a rule of measure: with what judgment you judge, you will be judged, and with what measure you mete it will be measured back. The standard a man uses on his brother is the standard the Father uses on him. Sirach had it in the Hebrew library long before the Sermon on the Mount: the revenger writes his own sentence.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:1 — *He that revengeth shall find vengeance from Yahuah (God).* Measure for measure: *with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again* (Matthew 7:2).

apoc_text: If he that is but flesh nourish hatred, who will intreat for pardon of his sins?
old_note: *If he that is but flesh nourish hatred, who will intreat for pardon of his sins?* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 28:5 names the beam-out-first prerequisite for the brother-mote-removal at Matt 7:5. The hatred-nourishing disciple cannot ask the Father's pardon for his own sins — and so cannot rightly help the brother with his. The wisdom-stream had already named the heart-clearing prerequisite the gospel formalizes; Matt 7:5 walks the same architecture into the just-judgment grammar.
new_note: *If he that is but flesh nourish hatred, who will intreat for pardon of his sins?* (Ecclesiasticus 28:5). *Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother’s eye.* (Matthew 7:5). Sirach asks who will plead for the pardon of a man who is only flesh and yet nurses hatred. Yahusha (Jesus) tells the man with the beam in his own eye to get it out first, and then he will see clearly to help his brother with the mote. The two belong together: the one nursing hatred cannot ask the Father's pardon for himself, and so he cannot rightly help a brother with his fault either. The beam comes out first, and the hatred is the beam.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:5 — *If he that is but flesh nourish hatred, who will intreat for pardon of his sins?.* The beam that comes out first (Matthew 7:5); hatred nursed in the heart leaves no one to plead for the man's own pardon.

apoc_text: Whoso teaches a fool is as one that glueth a potsherd together, and as he that waketh one from a sound sleep.
old_note: *Whoso teaches a fool is as one that glueth a potsherd together, and as he that waketh one from a sound sleep.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 22:7 names the wisdom-not-for-fools architecture the gospel's pearls-before-swine teaching walks. The wisdom-stream identifies the futility of teaching the one who cannot receive — the potsherd cannot be glued, the sleeper cannot be roused. Matt 7:6 binds the same architecture as a kingdom-citizens discrimination-of-audience commandment.
new_note: *Whoso teaches a fool is as one that glueth a potsherd together, and as he that waketh one from a sound sleep.* (Ecclesiasticus 22:7). *Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.* (Matthew 7:6). Sirach says teaching a fool is like gluing a broken pot back together, or waking a man out of a dead sleep — the effort does not hold. Yahusha (Jesus) says it as a command: do not give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine, because they will trample them and turn and rend you. Both know that some hearers cannot receive, and that the holy thing is wasted and the teacher is harmed when it is pressed on them. The proclamation goes out broadly, but the pursuit ends where the rejection lands.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 22:7 — *Whoso teaches a fool is as one that glueth a potsherd together.* The futility of teaching the one who cannot receive; *neither cast ye your pearls before swine* (Matthew 7:6).

apoc_text: He that telleth a tale to a fool speaks to one in a slumber: when he has told his tale, he will say, What is the matter?
old_note: *He that telleth a tale to a fool speaks to one in a slumber: when he has told his tale, he will say, What is the matter?* Sirach 22:8 names the don't-cast-words-on-the-unreceptive architecture in the wisdom-stream's register. Matt 7:6's *give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine* walks the same teaching at the holy-vs-dogs / pearls-vs-swine intensification. The Hebrew library had been naming the discernment of audience for centuries; the gospel locks it as a kingdom-citizens commandment.
new_note: *He that telleth a tale to a fool speaks to one in a slumber: when he has told his tale, he will say, What is the matter?* (Ecclesiasticus 22:8). *Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.* (Matthew 7:6). Sirach says telling a tale to a fool is talking to a man asleep — when you have finished he asks what you were saying. Yahusha (Jesus) sharpens that into a command about the holy things: do not cast pearls before swine, who will trample them and turn on you. The wisdom book had been teaching discernment of the hearer for centuries; the gospel makes it a rule for the citizens of the kingdom. We speak the truth wherever the Father sends us, and when it is refused we shake the dust off and go on.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 22:8 — *He that telleth a tale to a fool speaks to one in a slumber.* Discernment of the hearer, made a kingdom rule in Matthew 7:6.

apoc_text: Wisdom is glorious, and never fadeth away: yes, she is easily seen of them that love her, and found of such as seek her.
old_note: *Wisdom is glorious, and never fadeth away: yes, she is easily seen of them that love her, and found of such as seek her.* Wisdom of Solomon 6:12 names the seekers-find-wisdom architecture explicitly — wisdom is found of such as seek her. Matt 7:7's *seek, and ye shall find* walks the same wisdom-stream teaching at the kingdom-citizens prayer-confidence level. The Father gives the good gift (Luke 11:13 names the Ruach HaKodesh as the central good-thing) to those who ask, seek, and knock; the wisdom-stream had been naming the same seekers-find principle in the Hebrew library long before.
new_note: *Wisdom is glorious, and never fadeth away: yes, she is easily seen of them that love her, and found of such as seek her.* (Wisdom of Solomon 6:12). *Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you:* (Matthew 7:7). Wisdom is found of such as seek her. The King's three verbs, ask, seek, knock, carry the same promise: it will be given, you will find, it will be opened. Solomon adds that she is easily seen of them that love her, which means the seeking is not a long climb but a turning toward what is already in view. The Father gives the good gift to those who ask, and Luke names the gift as the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit) (Luke 11:13), which is the spirit of wisdom Solomon himself prayed for.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 6:12 — *she is easily seen of them that love her, and found of such as seek her.* Seek and ye shall find (Matthew 7:7) is the promise Solomon wrote about wisdom first.

apoc_text: She preventeth them that desire her, in making herself first known to them.

new_note: *She preventeth them that desire her, in making herself first known to them.* (Wisdom of Solomon 6:13). *Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you:* (Matthew 7:7). Preventeth in the old sense means goes before. Wisdom does not wait to be caught; she goes out ahead of those who desire her and makes herself known first. That is what the King's ask, seek, knock rests on: the disciple is not climbing up to a Father who has to be found, he is knocking on a door the Father is already standing behind. The asking is answered, the seeking finds, the knocking opens, because the one being sought came out to meet the seeker before the seeker set out.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 6:13 — *She preventeth them that desire her, in making herself first known to them.* Wisdom goes before those who desire her; the Father answers ask, seek, knock (Matthew 7:7) because he came out to meet the seeker first.

Matt 7:16-20's *by their fruits ye shall know them* walks the same architecture at the false-prophet diagnostic level. new_note: *The fruit declareth if the tree have been dressed; so is the utterance of a conceit in the heart of man.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:6). *Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?* (Matthew 7:16). Sirach says the fruit tells you whether the tree was dressed, and a man's speech tells you what is in his heart. Yahusha (Jesus) gives the same test for recognizing false prophets: you will know them by their fruits, because thorns do not yield grapes. The test was not new when he gave it; the wise in Yashar'el (Israel) had been teaching it for generations. What the gospel does is hand it to every disciple as the way to know a teacher, so that no one has to be fooled by the costume if he will look at the fruit.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 27:6 — *The fruit declareth if the tree have been dressed.* The fruit shows the tree, the speech shows the heart; the same test Yahusha (Jesus) gives at Matthew 7:16, *ye shall know them by their fruits*.

new_note: *Praise no man before you hear him speak; for this is the trial of men.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:7). *Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.* (Matthew 7:20). Sirach says do not praise a man until you have heard him speak, because that is where men are tried. Yahusha (Jesus) closes his warning about false prophets the same way: by their fruits you shall know them. A prophet's teaching is his fruit, and a teaching that voids the commandments of Yahuah (God) names the wolf no matter what signs he carries, because Deuteronomy 13 had already said the sign does not excuse the leading away. Hear him speak first; then you know what he is.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 27:7 — *Praise no man before you hear him speak.* The man is tried in his speaking; *by their fruits ye shall know them* (Matthew 7:20), and a teacher's teaching is his fruit.

apoc_text: As timber girt and bound together in a building cannot be loosed with shaking: so the heart that is stablished by advised counsel shall fear at no time.
old_note: *As timber girt and bound together in a building cannot be loosed with shaking: so the heart that is stablished by advised counsel shall fear at no time.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 22:16 names the heart-stablished-by-counsel-cannot-be-shaken architecture — the wisdom-stream's direct parallel to the gospel's rock-foundation-of-the-wise-builder teaching. Matt 7:24-25's house-upon-the-rock that does not fall when the rain and floods come walks the same architecture: the hearer-and-doer's heart-foundation is stablished by the counsel of the King's sayings, and the building does not fall.
new_note: *As timber girt and bound together in a building cannot be loosed with shaking: so the heart that is stablished by advised counsel shall fear at no time.* (Ecclesiasticus 22:16). *Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:* (Matthew 7:24). Sirach says a heart established by sound counsel is like timber girded and bound into a building — shake it and it does not come loose, so it fears nothing. Yahusha (Jesus) says the wise man is the one who hears his sayings and does them, and he likens him to a house built on a rock. The counsel that establishes the heart is the King's sayings, and the doing of them is what binds the timber. Hearing alone leaves the building loose.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 22:16 — *so the heart that is stablished by advised counsel shall fear at no time.* The hearer and doer who built on the rock (Matthew 7:24) has the heart Sirach describes.

apoc_text: A heart settled upon a thought of understanding is as a fair plaistering on the wall of a gallery.
old_note: *A heart settled upon a thought of understanding is as a fair plaistering on the wall of a gallery.* Sirach 22:17 names the heart-settled-on-understanding architecture — the foundation of the wise. Matt 7:24's wise-man-who-heareth-AND-doeth walks the same Hebrew library architecture: the kingdom-citizens hearer-and-doer settles his heart on the King's sayings (the heart-Torah of the Sermon) and the resulting building stands.
new_note: *A heart settled upon a thought of understanding is as a fair plaistering on the wall of a gallery.* (Ecclesiasticus 22:17). *Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:* (Matthew 7:24). Sirach says a heart settled on a thought of understanding is like fine plaster on the wall of a gallery — finished, smooth, holding. Yahusha (Jesus) says the wise man is the one who hears his sayings and does them, and likens him to a house built on rock. The settled heart and the house on rock are the same man: his heart has come to rest on the King's words, and the building he is stands.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 22:17 — *A heart settled upon a thought of understanding.* The settled heart is the hearer and doer of Matthew 7:24.

apoc_text: Pales set on an high place will never stand against the wind: so a fearful heart in the imagination of a fool cannot stand against any fear.
old_note: *Pales set on an high place will never stand against the wind: so a fearful heart in the imagination of a fool cannot stand against any fear.* Sirach 22:18 names the inverse: the fool's heart cannot stand against the wind. Matt 7:25 contrasts the same architecture by inversion at v.27 — the foolish man's house on the sand falls when the rain descended and the floods came and the winds blew. The Hebrew library named the wind-against-the-foolish architecture; the gospel locks the diagnostic at the hearer-without-the-doing level.
new_note: *Pales set on an high place will never stand against the wind: so a fearful heart in the imagination of a fool cannot stand against any fear.* (Ecclesiasticus 22:18). *And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.* (Matthew 7:25). Sirach gives the opposite picture: pales set on a height will never stand against the wind, and the fearful heart of a fool cannot stand against any fear. Matthew says the rain came down, the floods came, the winds blew and beat on the house, and it did not fall because it stood on rock. The same wind that cannot move the house on the rock blows the pales flat. The difference is not the wind but the foundation, and the foundation is hearing and doing.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 22:18 — *so a fearful heart in the imagination of a fool cannot stand against any fear.* The wind of Matthew 7:25 that cannot move the house on the rock blows the pales flat.

apoc_text: Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning.
old_note: *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 36:11 names the gathering-of-all-the-tribes architecture explicitly as the wisdom-stream's prayer-petition to the Most High. Matt 8:11's *many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Avraham (Abraham), and Yitschaq (Isaac), and Ya'aqov (Jacob), in the kingdom of heaven* walks the gathering-of-the-scattered-seed architecture the Hebrew library had been praying for; the *many from east and west* are the scattered seed of all twelve tribes returning to inherit, NOT the Christian-replacement-of-the-Jews construct.
new_note: *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning.* (Ecclesiasticus 36:11). *And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven.* (Matthew 8:11). Sirach prays for all the tribes of Jacob to be gathered and given back their inheritance as from the beginning, twelve tribes and not two. Yahusha (Jesus) says many will come from east and west and sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom. The many from east and west are the children of those three fathers coming home from where they were scattered, which is exactly what Sirach asked for. They are not a new people put in the seat of Yashar'el (Israel); they are the tribes of Jacob taking their own seats at their fathers' table.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 36:11 — *Gather all the tribes of Jacob together, and inherit you them, as from the beginning..* The many from east and west (Matthew 8:11) are the tribes coming home to their fathers' table.

apoc_text: O Yahuah (God), have mercy upon the people that is called by your name, and upon Yashar'el (Israel), whom you have named your firstborn.
old_note: *O Yahuah (God), have mercy upon the people that is called by your name, and upon Yashar'el (Israel), whom you have named your firstborn.* Sirach 36:12 names the firstborn-people architecture — Yashar'el (Israel) as the people named the Most High's firstborn. The Hebrew library's prayer for the gathering rests on the covenant-firstborn standing; Matt 8:11 walks the same architecture at the King's own naming of the gathering-of-the-patriarchs' seed.
